q: Which virus, spread by mealybug, is the chief limit on vineyard longevity in the Cape, forcing replanting long before vines reach old-vine status?
exp: Leafroll delays and prevents ripening, drops yields and reddens the foliage, and the mealybug vector spreads it block to block; the practical result has been a replant cycle closer to 15–20 years than 50. That is exactly why the Old Vine Project's 35-year certified blocks are so scarce and so prized — surviving old vines are usually virus-free by luck of clean plant material and isolation. Understanding leafroll explains why the Cape's old-vine story is a rescue operation, not an inheritance.

q: The Cape's 'coffee' or 'mocha' Pinotage style is produced by:
opts: co-fermenting Pinotage with roasted malt adjuncts
extended stem contact to lift roasted pyrazines
a proprietary Pinotage clone selected in Robertson
heavily charred new oak staves and high-toast barrels
exp: The mocha character is oak-derived — furfural and related volatiles from very high-toast wood, usually in the form of staves or chips rather than expensive barrels, often with a little residual sugar. Diemersfontein's 2001 bottling launched the style and it now sells enormously, especially domestically. Know it and be able to separate it cleanly from the serious Pinotage argument made by Kanonkop, Beyers Truter's legacy and Alheit-era old-vine thinking; conflating the two is a common tasting-note error.

q: What does the numbered seal on a South African bottle's neck certify, and from what year has it been issued?
accept: sustainability seal with a unique traceable number
wo certification plus ipw sustainable production
integrity seal traceable to the vineyard
ans: The Integrity & Sustainability seal, from 2010: it certifies the WO claims (origin, vintage, variety) together with compliance with the Integrated Production of Wine sustainability scheme, and carries a unique number traceable online back to the vineyard
exp: South Africa was the first country to put a mandatory-in-practice, fully traceable sustainability guarantee on the bottle, and roughly 95% of certified wine carries it. It is worth citing on a floor: the seal answers both 'is the origin claim true' and 'was it farmed responsibly' with one scannable number — a genuine competitive advantage the Cape rarely markets hard enough.

q: Mendoza's Uco Valley subzones Gualtallary and Altamira are prized for which soil feature?
ans: Calcareous (caliche) deposits over alluvial stone — chalky-textured Malbec
exp: Catena's Adrianna vineyard ('the Grand Cru of South America') sits at ~1,450 m in Gualtallary.

q: What is a 'parral' in Argentine viticulture?
ans: The high pergola trellis — historically for Criolla volume and hail/heat protection
exp: Modern quality vineyards mostly converted to VSP espalier.

exp: With hail ('piedra'), the region's two weather demons; nets shade a third of top vineyards.

q: Catena Zapata's high-altitude research argued which effect of UV light at 1,500 m?
accept: thicker skins more tannin and aroma
ans: Intense UV thickens skins — more tannin, color and floral aromatics at altitude
exp: Laura Catena's Catena Institute published the science behind 'high-altitude Malbec'.

q: Bonarda in Argentina is which French grape?
ans: Douce Noir (Corbeau de Savoie; California's Charbono)

q: Chile's 2011 coastal/entre-cordilleras/Andes labeling law lets producers add what to a label?
ans: 'Costa', 'Entre Cordilleras' or 'Andes' — a west-east climate axis over the old north-south DOs
exp: Because Casablanca-coast and Maipo-Andes differ more than Maipo and Maule do.

q: Which Maipo subzone at the Andes' feet is called the 'Pauillac of South America'?
exp: Almaviva, Don Melchor, Viñedo Chadwick — the 2004 Berlin Tasting's winners grew here.

q: Itata and Bío Bío's revival centers on which two historic grapes?
ans: País (Listán Prieto) and Cinsault — plus Muscat, dry-farmed bush vines
exp: The 16th-century mission grape reborn as natural-wine darling.

q: Chile's phylloxera status and its viticultural consequence:
ans: Phylloxera never established — most vines grow own-rooted
exp: Desert, Andes, Pacific and Patagonia quarantine the country naturally.

q: Uruguay's Tannat softens relative to Madiran chiefly because of:
ans: The humid Atlantic maritime climate (and massal 'Harriague' vine heritage)
exp: Basque immigrant Pascual Harriague planted it in the 1870s.

q: Match the Chilean valley to its calling card.
ans: Casablanca–coastal whites · Apalta–Carmenère/Syrah · Limarí–limestone Chard · Maule–VIGNO
exp: VIGNO: the old-vine Carignan compact — Chile's first terroir brand.

q: Argentina's Denominación de Origen Controlada system currently recognises which appellations?
opts: One: Luján de Cuyo, created in 1989
Two: Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael
Three: Luján de Cuyo, Maipú and San Rafael
exp: Only two DOCs exist, and neither is the fashionable name. Luján de Cuyo came first (1989, formalised under Law 25.163) and San Rafael followed. Gualtallary and Paraje Altamira are Geographic Indications (IGs), a separate and much larger register — the confusion is worth fixing, because the prestige of Argentine wine sits almost entirely in the IG system while the DOC tier stayed commercially inert.

q: Chilean law requires a varietally labelled wine to contain at least what proportion of the named grape?
exp: 75% is the domestic legal floor, and the same 75% applies to vintage and to stated origin. But the EU and the US both demand 85%, so almost every Chilean bottle you will ever see is made to 85% — which is why the textbook figure and the shelf reality disagree. Quote the law, then note the export practice.
